findings.title: A flood that arrives late meets the caller's first dial break inside the destination's T_ARM watch, or while the classifier is still busy. The port is re-seized mid-digit and a monitor claims a wrong number.
findings.mechanism:
Nothing in the RTL bounds how old a flood is when it reaches an exchange.

Per hop, the forwarder adds 12.1-13.9 ms (measured, far M in to far M out). That is:
- a classifier read, ~1.5 ms;
- a sweep of 64 reads on the stride of 9, 9 ms (net_unit.v:750-777);
- the CONFIRM pass, 1 ms (:779-785);
- the cable-B write, 0.3-0.7 ms;
- the incoming's next turn.

The hop grows to 30-31 ms when the seizure waits behind another seizure's T_ARM watch: the classifier takes nothing outside C_IDLE (:283-284), and C_HOLD lasts T_ARM+1..2 ms (:584-588). It grows to 18-25 ms when the forward waits for an origin sweep: F_WANT yields to N_WANT (:714-719, :847-852).

At the destination:
- The watch treats ANY M-low sample within T_ARM+1..2 ms of the hold write as the seizure dying (:586), and C_UNHOLD writes the hold away (:590-594).
- If that low was the caller's first break, the port's own (fm && !m) term (port.v:147) keeps it BUSY through the break. The M-low samples clear st (:566-567).
- When M returns with BUSY=0, cls_seen re-classifies the port as a FRESH seizure (:283-284). A second monitor is attached mid-digit (:612-615); it counts e short (:635-642) and claims (:656-671).
- R_GONE drops the first forward's legs (:688-689, :694-698), and a new forward goes out from mid-digit (:616-621). Every exchange downstream is therefore also re-seized mid-digit.

The variant with a busy classifier (another seizure's watch in progress) ends the same way: the port is first seen at the end of the first break.
findings.trigger:
tb_fx sc6, real timers. B = 2 3.
- A flood arrives on E30 112 ms after its origin seized: about 9 nominal hops, or about 8 with one transit behind a watch.
- The far caller dialled 1 3 3 2 1. The first break of e starts 129 ms after the origin's seizure, which is past the 128 ms guard and so legal. That is 17 ms after the flood reached B.
- (a) No other traffic.
- (b) Another flood arrives on S41 1 ms earlier.
findings.consequence: B claims a call dialled to exchange 3 3 and rings B21: a wrong number the caller cannot see. The first, correct monitor lets go at e=3 while the re-attached one claims. Downstream exchanges also receive a mid-digit re-flood.
findings.realistic:
Survives real timing: the runs used real timers. The upstream latency is modelled as a delay before the far M rises; it is the sum of measured per-hop latencies.

It needs a fast dialer: the first break of e must come within ~0-20 ms after the origin's guard expires. The origin's r_brk comes HIT = 8 ms into a break, so a break may start ~120 ms after the seizure. That is an inter-digit pause of ~0.27 s: rare for people, plausible for an autodialer or a data card pulsing DTR.

The destination must be reached at least ~100 ms after the origin seized:
- about 9 hops at the measured 13 ms a hop with no other traffic;
- about 7-8 hops with any one load event: a coincident seizure at the destination (measured margin under 1 ms at 92 ms), a transit behind a watch (+18 ms), or behind an origin sweep (+6-12 ms).

network.md 3.2 allows 'about eight hops' on the 128 ms tap, and the net_unit.v header says ten at 9 ms a hop. At that envelope the margin is ~8 ms nominal and negative with one load event.

findings.title: A resolver whose incoming trunk's link goes down (LTU/MF8 MUTE_BLK) outlives its call. Its stale legs are later cut, re-pointed or re-seized.
findings.mechanism:
When a local trunk's link dies, local_trunk.v:188-189 drops A and raises MUTE_BLK, and port.v:147 makes MUTE_BLK part of every port's BUSY.

R_GONE fires only when the incoming reads BUSY=0 (net_unit.v:688-689), so it cannot fire for the whole outage. Meanwhile the incoming's latch released itself T_REL after its A fell, and every leg released itself (their E fell).

The resolver keeps rs_busy, rs_held and rs_leg:
- Its old legs stay `mine` (:435-436).
- R_LEG still fires on ANY M on an old leg (:684-687). w_res then drops the other old legs and writes the way back onto the dead incoming (:691-705).
- At the mend, R_GONE drops every old leg (:694-698).

All of these writes land on ports that other calls now use.
findings.trigger:
tb_fx sc2, real timers. A W neighbour's seizure on LTU channel B10 is forwarded into E30 and S40. Then the LTU cable is cut for longer than 256 ms.
- var0: during the outage B20 keys 1; its flood takes E30 and S40, the free old legs. The cable is mended while B20 is dialling.
- var1: during the outage the E neighbour seizes E30 to call B21. The cable is mended during that call.
findings.consequence:
The resolver is lost for the whole outage; with NRES=2 that is half of a transit's forwarding.

var0: at the mend the stale R_GONE re-points B20's two live trunks to 00, cutting its flood mid-dial. When the E party claims anyway, B20 hears it but the E party hears nothing. B's classifier then takes the E party's claim level on the now non-BUSY E30 as a fresh incoming seizure, monitors it and floods it W and S: a phantom flood.

var1: the stale R_LEG re-points the dead B10 at E30. After the mend the W neighbour sees a seizure on its channel 0 carrying the E caller's hook and voice for the whole E-B21 call. A real W neighbour would hold it, monitor it and forward it through its own network for the call's duration; nothing times out a steady M at a monitor or a resolver.

Everything heals only when the unrelated call ends.
findings.realistic: Real timers, as run. It needs any LTU or MF8 outage longer than T_REL (256 ms) that starts while a forward from that link is held. That probability is roughly the link's forward occupancy at the transit: ~5-25% of such outages at a busy hub. var1 is the likely outcome once the old legs are reused before the mend. A baseband cut has no MUTE and is not affected.

findings.title: Every forward, even a chain's one-leg patch, needs a free resolver and an idle forwarder at the moment of classification. Otherwise the flood silently stops here.
findings.mechanism:
A seizure is forwarded only if fst == F_IDLE && rs_free_any at C_ACT (net_unit.v:616-617). There is no retry: the seizure is held (:609-611) and counted in n_nofwd (:506-507, :545).

F_WRITE allocates a resolver for one-leg forwards too (:737-741, rs_two). A resolver is freed only by:
- R_LEG, a claim coming back through this exchange;
- rs_mine, a claim here;
- R_GONE, the incoming reading free T_REL after its origin let go.

So each resolver is held for the flood's e b dialling (2.0-3.8 s, mean 2.7 s) plus 0.26 s when the claim is made elsewhere.

This contradicts network.md 3.2 on two points: 'no resolver free: patch into the first direction found, as a chain would', and 'a transit on a chain ... holds nothing'.
findings.trigger:
tb_fx sc4: floods on E30, S41, W12 and N77, 40 ms apart, at a four-direction transit with NRES=2 and NMON=2.

findings.consequence:
In sc4 the third and fourth floods are held BUSY but never passed on, and not watched either (both monitors are taken). Their callers hear cannot-complete only T_CLAIM (2 s) after b, about 5 s after the key, and every channel and resolver upstream stays held until then.

In sc5d the second flood is lost even though a resolver is free: the forwarder was still sweeping after waiting 10.5 ms for the origin.

Arithmetic (Erlang B, 2.9 s holds, 48 lines an exchange, 3 calls a line an hour; every flood passes every transit):
- 8 exchanges, 30% leaving: 0.24 E, 2.3% of floods not forwarded.
- 8 exchanges, 50% leaving: 5.6%.
- 20 exchanges: 0.66 E, 11.6% with NRES=2, 2.5% with 3, 0.4% with 4.

Behaviour at the limit is graceful: nothing stays stuck, a freed resolver is reused at once, and everything is idle after release. It is slow, though, and doomed floods hold resources upstream.
findings.realistic:
Yes, at real timers.

The forwarder-busy loss needs an origin sweep ahead of a pair of floods arriving within ~20 ms. At real timers the ~19 ms T_ARM watch otherwise keeps classifications apart. At scale 8 the watch is only ~4 ms, so scale-8 load studies overstate this loss.

findings.title: Glare on a forward's leg: R_LEG takes the far exchange's own seizure as the claim and joins two callers, and the transit counts nothing
findings.mechanism:
The resolver watch sets R_LEG on any M on a held leg (net_unit.v:684-687), and w_res then re-points the incoming at that leg and drops the others (:691-705).

There is a window of ~1-3.5 ms between the forwarder's CONFIRM sample of a leg (:779-785) and the leg's write landing plus one turn. In that window the far exchange can seize the same channel for its own origin call or forward. It hunts from the other end, so this needs the link's last free channel.

The far M is then indistinguishable from a claim. Only the origin counts glare (:803); a transit has no n_glare or EV_GLARE path.
findings.trigger: tb_fx sc3: a flood arrives on E30. B's forward confirms S40 free (hst=CONFIRM, h_n=40). The S neighbour seizes S40 for its own call before B's leg write lands.

The E flood's caller and the S neighbour's caller are joined both ways (E30 <-> S40), and the flood's other legs, W10 and N74, are dropped. n_glare stays 0 and no EV_GLARE is sent.

The S origin takes our caller's M as its own claim; it is counted there only if inside its guard. Each origin then connects its caller. Neither dialled the other.
findings.realistic: Yes, at real timers. The per-link condition is the same as the documented residual glare: the last free channel, both ends within a few ms. But a flood seizes a channel on every link of the tree, so the exposure per call is multiplied by the number of links it crosses. Order of magnitude: 1e-4 per call in a loaded network (arithmetic).

findings.title: F_WRITE ignores f_cancel. A seizure on port 77 that dies in the last CONFIRM sample leaves 77 and its one leg BUSY for good and a resolver held.
findings.mechanism:
C_UNHOLD sets f_cancel (net_unit.v:593), but only F_WANT (:714) and F_HUNT at h_done (:722) read it. F_WRITE (:725-743) and w_fwd (:492-493) do not.

The sweep's last read is always port 70, and it ends in port 00's bit-time. So CONFIRM always visits exactly 00..77, and h_done falls on 77's sample.

A seizure on 77 whose first M-low sample is that one gets its unhold queued first, because w_cls outranks w_fwd (:488). The forward follows it. For a one-leg forward, the way back (:732-736) then re-holds 77 BUSY, listening to the leg.

At real timers the watch (17-18 ms) outlasts a forward (~11-12 ms), so the window exists. At scale 8 (watch ~4 ms) it does not.

Neither port can ever release itself: 77 gets no fM edge and its leg no fE edge, so both stay BUSY with bsy=1. The resolver waits for an R_GONE that cannot come.

It heals only when the leg's far exchange seizes that channel. R_LEG then frees the resolver, and that neighbour's call is patched straight through B to the N neighbour; B's classifier never sees it, because the leg is BUSY. The pair clears when that call ends.

findings.title: Scale-8 benches cannot judge the forwarder: the unscaled sweep is set against T_ARM, T_REL and a guard 8x shorter
findings.mechanism:
At scale 8 the benches get the forwarder's timing wrong in four ways:
- The classifier's T_ARM watch (C_HOLD, net_unit.v:584-588) is ~4 ms, shorter than a forward (10.5-12 ms). F_WRITE therefore never lands inside it, and the port-77 race cannot appear.
- Any two seizures ~5-11 ms apart lose the second to a busy forwarder (:616). At real timers the ~19 ms watch spaces them, and only an origin sweep brings the loss back.
- T_REL (32 ms) is shorter than a loaded hop (up to ~31 ms, measured 5b), so a forward can be written after its incoming has released.
- The guard (16 ms) is shorter than one hop (12-14 ms plus detection), so the late-flood wrong number cannot be judged. The benches rely on the 100 ms digit pause instead.
findings.trigger: tb_net, tb_chain, tb_lnet, tb_lfull, tb_lchain and any scale-8 load study.
findings.consequence: Scale-8 runs overstate n_nofwd (forwarder busy), cannot show the port-77 stuck state, and cannot show the guard-budget wrong number.
findings.realistic: This is a property of the benches, not of the RTL.
findings.evidence: run_fx_sc5.log hop latencies (12.1-13.9 / 30.4-31.4 / 18.4-25.5 ms) against the scale-8 timers T_ARM 2, T_REL 32, guard 16. The late-flood and outage findings above only appear at real timers.
findings.fix: Study the forwarder at real timers. tb_fx is one exchange with its far ends driven by the bench and runs ~30 ms of simulated time per wall-clock second. Alternatively, give the benches a knob that scales the sweep's step with the timers.

findings.title: An unjumpered ring is bounded only by resources, and its lap copies are late floods
findings.mechanism:
STRAP_N is the only loop breaker (net_unit.v:505, :616-618). It matches network.md 3.3.

Nothing recognises a flood returning to its own origin exchange: it arrives on a different trunk, which is not `mine`. There is no hop limit either. A seizure keeps circling until one of these stops it:
- at each exchange the forwarder is busy or both resolvers are held (so at most NRES laps);
- a link runs out of channels.

Each lap copy holds a channel per link and a resolver and a monitor per exchange until the claim plus T_REL. Each lap arrives ~N x 13 ms later. In rings of about 8 or more exchanges a lap copy reaches an exchange after the caller's first break, which is the late-flood mechanism above.
findings.trigger: A ring of N exchanges with no STRAP_N jumper anywhere.
findings.consequence: Every call burns roughly NRES laps x N channels and all resolvers. There are double claims (a cannot-complete race), and in large rings late copies can be counted short, which could give a wrong-number claim.
findings.realistic: Only when the ring is misconfigured. The late-copy wrong number rests on the reproduced late-flood mechanism, but was not simulated as a ring.
findings.evidence: Reasoning from the code and from the reproduced late-flood mechanism. Not simulated.
findings.fix: The jumper is the design; add a commissioning check (one test call per ring). A cheap in-RTL guard would be to refuse to forward a seizure that arrives more than ~100 ms after the exchange's own origin seized with the same caller. That is not free, so documentation plus a bench is the recommendation.

sound.claim: The origin and the forwarder never pick the same trunk, so neither hijacks the other's latch.
sound.why: There is one sweep engine and it is strictly sequential (h_owner). A hunter's writes land 0.3-0.7 ms after its h_done: in sc5c the origin's four writes landed at +0.28 to +0.69 ms. The other hunter's CONFIRM visits every candidate at least 9 ms later and drops any that are BUSY. `mine` covers o_cand and f_cand from h_done until the write, and d_held and rs_held after it (net_unit.v:429-438). In sc5c, back to back, the origin took 74, 40, 31 and 10 and the forward took 75, 41 and 11 (run_fx_sc5.log:282-320).

sound.claim: There is no gap between CONFIRM and `mine`, so a candidate is never classified as an incoming seizure.
sound.why: The sweep's last read is always port 70, and its word ends in 00's bit-time. CONFIRM therefore visits exactly 00..77, and h_done falls on 77's sample. N_SEIZE's and F_WRITE's `mine` terms are live two ticks later, about 62 ticks before the next sample of any port. A far M that rises after a candidate's CONFIRM visit can only be glare (see leg-glare-joins-uncounted).

sound.claim: The mini marker never takes a free trunk out from under a hunt.
sound.why: It reads the word of every M and not-BUSY port and leaves a flood trunk alone (mini_marker S_READ: rd_trunk -> S_IDLE). It refuses a dialled trunk (S_READ -> NOGO). It writes a trunk only through att, which means a claimed trunk.

sound.claim: No deadlock or starvation between the origin and the forwarder over the sweep.
sound.why: F_WANT yields only to an origin in N_WANT, which happens once per call because there is one register. An origin waits at most one forward sweep (about 12 ms, measured). N_WANT waits only on hst, and F_WANT only on hst and nst, so there is no circular wait. Measured back to back in sc5c and sc5d.

sound.claim: w_res and w_claim push slots never collide, and room is always sufficient.
sound.why: There is at most one leg per direction, and at most 3 legs (the incoming's direction is excluded). w_res uses slots 0-3 for legs and slot 4 for the way back; w_claim uses slot 0 for CLAIM and slots 1-4 for legs. cnt_res = 4 covers at most 3 writes, and cnt_claim is at most 4. Two resolvers never share rs_in: R_GONE frees the old one at the incoming's first BUSY=0 sample, which comes before any re-classified forward, since that needs a read and a sweep.

sound.claim: Several resolvers acting at once are serialised correctly.
sound.why: rs_act1 takes one resolver per tick and the others wait. w_res is outranked only by single-tick pushes. In sc4 the claim on one resolver freed it while the other held on.

sound.claim: A forward of a trunk already claimed here cannot happen.
sound.why: A claim needs e and b to be counted: at least ~0.5 s after the seizure at real timers, ~90 ms scaled. A forward is written within ~12-25 ms (at most ~45 ms worst case). When the claim comes, rs_mine drops the forward's legs and frees its resolver.

sound.claim: In normal operation R_GONE is not masked by a re-seizure of the incoming.
sound.why: The resolver sees the incoming's first BUSY=0 sample after release; that is the same sample the classifier would act on, and any re-hold needs a read (at least 9 frames) first. R_GONE is masked only under MUTE (resolver-outlives-muted-incoming) and in the port-77 case.

sound.claim: In normal release, R_GONE's drop writes do not land on reused legs.
sound.why: Legs release within about 1 ms of the incoming, and the drops are queued within about 1 ms after that. A sweep needs its 1 ms CONFIRM after reading a port free before it can queue a write, so the window is at most ~0.1 ms and needs w_res delayed. It was not seen. My fix closes it anyway, since gone legs are never written.

sound.claim: STRAP_N implements network.md 3.3 exactly.
sound.why: A seizure is never forwarded onward from a jumpered link (:616) nor into one (fwd_mask, :505 and :618). An origin may still seize a jumpered link (h_mask 1111, :849). nf_busy excludes jumpered arrivals.

sound.claim: Fan-out resolution at a hub works.
sound.why: In sc4, three-leg forwards were written. The S40 leg's claim re-pointed E30 at it and dropped W10 and N74. The freed resolver was immediately reused by a fifth flood, and everything was idle after release. The run is PASS, identical with my fix.

sound.claim: Overload in this slice is graceful: no livelock, no thrash, no stuck state.
sound.why: Floods beyond NRES, or arriving while the forwarder is busy, are held but not forwarded, and nothing retries. They release with their origin (T_CLAIM + T_REL). sc4's idle check passed.

sound.claim: Keeping one candidate per direction at CONFIRM costs little.
sound.why: With the g ordering, a candidate lost at CONFIRM is almost always the link's last free channel, because the far end hunts from the other end. A fallback candidate would rarely find another.

sound.claim: Every sweep terminates.
sound.why: There are 64 steps, and the 00 step waits for 00's turn (:772-776), followed by 64 CONFIRM samples. A read cannot wait for ever: win counts down on every a_stb, and another reader's select delays it by at most a pass.

sound.claim: The unit's cable-B master behaves under forwarder traffic.
sound.why: Across all tb_fx runs, including the fix runs: no clash (nclash 0), no queue refusal (un_ovf 0), and fan-out writes of up to 4 words in one tick.

sound.claim: The one-leg forward (rs_two) is correct.
sound.why: Both latches are written at once, so a claim's backward A reaches the origin with no resolver action. The resolver it keeps is what lets a local claim drop the onward leg (rs_mine), as tb_chain exercises. The only cost is capacity, covered in forward-needs-resolver-and-idle-forwarder.

notes:
What I did: I read the snapshot only and never edited it. I studied the forwarder, the resolvers and the sweep with one new real-timer bench, work/audit/fwd/tb_fx.v. It is one exchange (B = 2 3, top_net, NRES 2, NMON 2):
- Its W direction is an LTU whose far unit is a bench-side local_trunk.
- Its E, S and N directions are baseband cards whose far ends are wires the bench drives (a_in, c_in, far clock) and reads (a_out, c_out).
- site_fx.v is site_net.v plus four clock outputs.
- B's internals are read hierarchically only for reporting.
- It runs at ~30 ms of simulated time per wall-clock second. Scenarios are selected with +sc, +var, +dly and +load.

Headline numbers, real timers:
- Hop latency, far M in to leg far M out: 12.1-13.9 ms nominal. The sweep is 9 ms of that, CONFIRM 1 ms, the classifier read ~1.5 ms.
- 30.4-31.4 ms behind another seizure's T_ARM watch.
- 18.4-25.5 ms behind an origin sweep.
- An origin sweep plus two floods 1 ms apart loses the second flood.

Capacity:
- The resolver pool (2) is the binding limit at a transit: roughly 2.3% of floods not forwarded at 8 exchanges and 30% leaving, 11.6% at 20 exchanges.
- The forwarder and the sweep are not bottlenecks at real timers. The sweep is ~10.5 ms per use; the forwarder is lost only behind an origin sweep.
- Behaviour at every limit I drove is graceful but slow: cannot-complete about T_CLAIM after b. There was no stuck state, except the link-outage and port-77 defects.

Safety:
- Reproduced a wrong number at real timers. A flood reaching an exchange ~110 ms after its origin seized, with the first dial break legally at 129 ms, is re-seized mid-digit by the T_ARM watch or a busy classifier. B then claimed a call dialled to 3 3 and rang B21. It sits at the documented 'about eight hops' envelope. The upstream path latency is modelled as a delay, using the measured per-hop latency.
- Reproduced glare on a forward's leg joining two callers, uncounted.

Liveness:
- Reproduced that a resolver whose incoming goes MUTE outlives its call, and that its stale writes cut, one-way or phantom-seize later calls.
- A fix copy (work/audit/fwd/rtl_fix/net_unit.v: rs_lb and rs_lf per leg, dissolve when every leg is gone, and F_WRITE honours f_cancel) passes the outage scenarios and regresses green on tb_fx sc4, tb_chain (32/32) and tb_lchain (48/48).

Overlaps with other slices:
- The port-77 f_cancel race was found and reproduced independently by the cableb slice (work/audit/cableb/tb_fcan.v); I cite its log.
- The classifier-latency part of the late-flood finding overlaps the cls slice's burst bench.
- The destination-watch re-seizure (C_UNHOLD, then re-classify mid-digit) is classifier territory, but it is what turns forwarder latency into a wrong number, so I report it here.
- The sc2 var1 FAIL 'B holds E30 as an incoming seizure' is a bench-check artefact (a one-leg forward re-points E30 at S40), not a defect.
- Monitors hold a steady-M seizure for ever: there is no timeout, so a phantom from a stale latch ties one up at every exchange it reaches. That belongs to the monitor slice.

The build directories were deleted; the logs and sources are kept. Rebuild with:

./sim.sh bash -c 'verilator --binary --timing -j 2 -Irtl -Wno-fatal --top-module tb_fx --Mdir work/audit/fwd/obj_fx -o tb_fx $(cat work/RTL.list) work/audit/fwd/site_fx.v work/audit/fwd/tb_fx.v'

findings.title: A link outage of 8-256 ms is a dial pulse to every monitor and register beyond it: a wrong number
findings.mechanism: A trunk card drops A the instant its link-up detector falls and raises it again when the link returns: baseband_card.v:109 (link_up = quiet < DEAD, 192 master ticks = 47 us of silence on the fifth conductor) and :154 (a_tx = a_s2 && link_up && settled); local_trunk.v:127/170/188 do the same for all eight channels (a_tx = live ? x_a : 0). The far port's release detector rides an outage shorter than T_REL (port.v:176-188), but every pulse counter reading that M counts it: a break of HIT (8 ms) or more is a pulse (pulse_rx.v:84). Before the claim those are the monitor cells (net_unit.v:316-320 pulse_rx on the cell's probe; 633-645 decide e and b on the count). After the claim it is the owner's register, which the marker attaches to the claimed trunk (mini_marker.v:305-319), and which reads the trunk's M. The origin's register reads its own caller, never the trunk, and nothing compares the two counts. An outage inside a digit adds a pulse; one in a pause adds a digit 1. network.md 1.1 (lines 71, 79) tells a carrier to 'let A fall' on link down, and bounds only lengthened makes and breaks, never an inserted one. monitor.md's two rules act only on the first digit heard.
findings.trigger: work/audit/proto/tb_pflap.v at REAL timers (HIT 8, ID 128, CLR 256, T_REL 256, guard 128, T_CLAIM 2000; dial 10 pps 60/40, 600 ms pauses). A = 2 1, B = 2 3, two baseband channels A11-B11, A12-B12. sc1: A20 dials 1 2 2 2 1 (exchange 22 exists nowhere); the cable (all five conductors, both channels) is out for 40 ms, starting 30 ms into the make after b's second pulse. sc2: A20 dials 1 2 3 2 1; B claims; the cable is out for 40 ms in the make after s's one pulse.
findings.consequence: sc1: B's monitor counts b = 3, B claims a call dialled to 22, A's origin takes the claim, and B's register reads 2 1 and connects B21. A20 dialled 22-21 and talks to 23-21. sc2: B's register counts s = 2 and B22 rings instead of B21. The caller gets no sign either way. Any link on the path counts, not only the origin's. An outage in the pause between the key and e makes every monitor beyond it read (1, e) as the code, i.e. the 10-17 range the numbering plan gives the backbone and hubs. On a local trunk one outage hits all eight channels' calls at once.
findings.realistic: Survives real timing: reproduced at real timers. It needs an outage of 8-256 ms on any link of the path while the caller is dialling e b (before the claim) or h s (after it), about 4-5 s per call. On copper in one room that is a disturbed connector or a clock-conductor glitch (DEAD is only 47 us). On MF8 (not in this RTL) it is a loss of frame lock that MUTEs A while the link re-syncs (network.md 1: 'MUTE clears the A hold'). Rare per call, but it is the one path to a wrong number that the guard and rule 1 do not address, and every link of every path is exposed.
findings.evidence: work/audit/proto/run_pflap.log. Control sc0 green ('control: nobody claims a call to exchange 22', 'control: A20 hears cannot-complete after the claim wait'). sc1: 'OBS 1990.0 ms cable cut for 40 ms' / 'OBS 2159.4 ms B raises att: a claim on B11' / 'OBS 2160.2 ms A's origin has its claim' / 'OBS 2600.0 ms b is in (A's register: 2 digits, 0022)' / 'OBS B21 rang 1, B22 rang 0; A claimed 1' / 'FAIL outage in b: nobody claims a call dialled to exchange 22' / 'FAIL outage in b: B21 (23-21, never dialled) does not ring'. sc2: 'OBS 3590.0 ms cable cut for 40 ms' / 'OBS B21 rang 0, B22 rang 1' / 'FAIL outage in s: B22 (never dialled) does not ring'. ('rang' = B's marker wrote the line BUSY, i.e. connected it.)
findings.fix: Make an outage a RELEASE, never a pulse. The trunk card POISONS itself on an outage of RIDE = 4 ms or more; RIDE is below HIT, so anything shorter can never count. While poisoned it holds A at 0 both ways, into its port and out to the far card, until the link is up AND its own port's A_RX has been idle for 300 ms (past T_REL and CLR). Both ends then release and their monitors and registers clear. An origin that still holds the trunk keeps its card poisoned, so the far end never sees a fresh seizure (finding link-return-fresh-seizure) and the origin times out at T_CLAIM. Cost: about half a '4040, a '74 and two gates per baseband card. For the local trunk, a poison bit per channel plus one shared timer, about 2 packages. The price is that an established call dies on any outage of 4 ms or more instead of clicking. TESTED in a copy, work/audit/proto/rtl_fix/baseband_card.v (RTL_fix.list), with the same bench: sc1 no claim, 'ok outage in b: nobody claims'. sc2 the claimed call is dropped: neither B21 nor B22 rings, so a failed call replaces the wrong line. sc3 no false claim. Both exchanges idle after each (work/audit/proto/run_pflap_fix.log). Not run against the tree's benches. Also add to network.md 1.1's carrier table: 'A must never show a break the caller did not make'.

findings.title: A link that returns while the caller is still dialling is a fresh seizure at the far end, counted from mid-number: a false claim
findings.mechanism: An outage of T_REL or more releases the far hold (port.v:176-194: the fM detector falls, rel clears the latch). Its monitor clears at CLR (net_unit.v:647-649), and st[] for the port is cleared by the M-down sample (net_unit.v:566-567). The origin sees no event: its trunk's M was 0 before any claim. It keeps the trunk listening to its caller (net_unit.v:811-815) and waits for T_CLAIM. When the link returns, the far port shows M with BUSY clear and st clear. cls_seen (net_unit.v:283-284) takes it as a new seizure: a hold, a new monitor and a new forward. The rise is real, so monitor.md rule 1 is met, and the origin's guard expired long ago. The new monitor counts the caller's remaining digits as e b.
findings.trigger: tb_pflap.v sc3, real timers: A (2 1) and B (2 3). A20 dials 1 2 2 3 1 (exchange 22: nobody). The cable is out for 500 ms starting 200 ms after e's first break, so e's two pulses are through, and it returns in the pause after e.
findings.consequence: B's new monitor reads b = 2 as e and h = 3 as b, and B (2 3) claims a call dialled to 22. A's origin takes that claim. B's register then gets s = 1 as its first digit, reads it as a key from a claimed trunk and refuses (mini_marker.v:423, NOGO with CLM), so A20 hears cannot-complete. With s = 2..7 instead, B's only register would sit on the call for NODIG (10 s) waiting for a digit that never comes, refusing every other claim and local caller meanwhile. The real owner, had it existed beyond B, never gets the call, because the flood beyond the outage was released.
findings.realistic: Reproduced at real timers. Needs an outage of 256 ms or more that ends while the caller is still dialling: a cable re-seated, or an MF8 link re-locking. Rarer than link-outage-dial-pulse; same family, same fix.
findings.evidence: work/audit/proto/run_pflap.log sc3: 'OBS 1200.0 ms cable cut for 500 ms' / 'OBS 1700.0 ms cable back' / 'OBS 2989.7 ms B raises att: a claim on B11' (= end of h's third pulse + ID 128) / 'OBS 2990.1 ms A's origin has its claim' / 'FAIL link back mid-dial: nobody claims a call dialled to exchange 22'. With the fixed card: 'OBS 4500.0 ms all dialled; B mon 00 reg 0; A claimed 0' / 'ok link back mid-dial: nobody claims' (run_pflap_fix.log).
findings.fix: Same card fix as link-outage-dial-pulse: the origin side's card stays poisoned while its port's A_RX is up, i.e. while the origin still has the caller on it. Tested: no false claim. A unit-side alternative is weaker: the classifier cannot tell a returning link from a new seizure, because the word read (net_unit.v:572-573) looks the same.

findings.title: A seizure with no origin behind it (one stuck A conductor) holds a monitor, a resolver and a channel on every link it floods, for good; the near end keeps seizing the dead channel
findings.mechanism: Nothing on the unit times out a monitor cell or a resolver. A cell is freed only by a decided digit or a 256 ms break (net_unit.v:633-649). A resolver is freed only by M on one of its legs (R_LEG) or by the incoming port's BUSY falling (R_GONE, net_unit.v:681-708). The only timers are the origin's (T_KEY, T_CLAIM, net_unit.v:876-882) and the classifier's T_ARM watch (584-588). A seizure whose M neither falls nor pulses has no origin to time it out. The link-up detector watches only the clock conductor (baseband_card.v:109; local_trunk.v:127/170), so an A conductor stuck at 1 reads as a live seizure: an open conductor into a fail-safe-high receiver (tb_lnet.v:57 models a cut exactly so), or a driver stuck on. At the other end the channel looks FREE, because the far hold sends no backward A. So the near origin's sweep, which keeps the lowest free trunk (or the highest with g; net_unit.v:759-766), picks that channel on every call, into a far port that is already BUSY with M up, where the new seizure is invisible.
findings.trigger: work/audit/proto/tb_pchain.v sc1 (scale 8; no timer is involved). A 2 2 is linked to B 2 3 on three baseband channels (A faces E, B faces W with g); B is linked to C 2 4 on one. The A conductor from A11 into B11 sticks at 1.
findings.consequence: B holds B11, a monitor and a resolver, and forwards over the only B-C channel; C holds C11 and a monitor. All of it is unchanged 1.1 s later (8.8 s real) and would stay so for ever. C is cut off from the network: its key finds no trunk and it gets cannot-complete at once. Every network call from A fails: A's key takes A11 (free at A, BUSY at B), so A20 cannot even reach its neighbour B, and it hears cannot-complete after T_CLAIM. B's calls to A still work, because B hunts W from the top. With NMON = NRES = 2, two such seizures reaching an exchange take both its monitors, and it can never claim again. A local trunk carries all eight channels' A on one conductor. One open conductor there is eight phantom seizures: at real timers the classifier's 18 ms T_ARM watch serialises them, so the forwarder is free for each until the two resolvers are gone. That takes both of B's monitors and resolvers, plus a channel, a monitor and a resolver at every exchange downstream of each of two phantom floods. No event word is sent and nothing alarms. Everything clears when the conductor is mended.
findings.realistic: Triggered by a single-conductor fault, which is plausible in a rack or on a cable. It does not depend on timer scaling. The effect is permanent and silent until repaired. The same missing timeout is reached from a local-trunk cut: MUTE_BLK keeps the incoming port BUSY, so R_GONE never comes (fwd slice, work/audit/fwd/run_fx_sc2var0.log 'FAIL the resolver let go of a forward whose incoming is dead'). A conductor stuck at 0 (fail-safe-low baseband receivers, baseband.md 3.3) does not leak, but gives the same black hole at the near origin.
findings.evidence: work/audit/proto/run_pchain.log sc1: 'OBS 100 ms after: ... B mon 01 res 01 ... B11->14 ... B14->11 bsy 1 | C ... mon 01' / 'OBS 1.1 s after (8.8 s real): (identical)' / 'FAIL a seizure nobody dials on does not hold a monitor or a resolver for good' / 'FAIL nor the B-C channel' / 'OBS C20 keys 1: C dirs 0000, hears s1 0 s0 1' / 'FAIL C can still reach the network' / 'OBS A20 keys 1: A dirs 0100, A11 busy 1 A12 busy 0' / 'OBS A20 dialled B: A claimed 0, hears s1 0 s0 1, B reg 0' / 'FAIL A20 can still reach its neighbour B' / 'ok B20 reaches A (B's glare order takes B13...)' / 'ok sc1: mended -- everything released' / 'ok after the mend A20 reaches C again'.
findings.fix: (a) A monitor timeout: a cell that has not decided e within about T_KEY (5 s) of its attach frees itself. The hold stays; the port is still up. Cost: a bit or two per cell on a shared slow counter, about half a package a cell. (b) A resolver timeout at about T_KEY + T_CLAIM (7-8 s) that drops the legs and frees itself, about half a package a resolver. (c) An event word for both, naming the port, so a stuck conductor alarms (counters.md). (d) At the origin, an EV_NOCLAIM event naming the trunk when T_CLAIM expires. Optionally a 6-bit 'failed last time' register the sweep skips, so one dead channel cannot take every call (the sweep already compares h_idx with candidates).

findings.title: Glare between a transit's forward and an origin makes the upstream call hostage to a stranger; the owner's own claim then releases the path under both callers
findings.mechanism: The forwarder hunts with the same sweep and the same per-candidate g compare as an origin (net_unit.v:759-766), so g protects it equally, and residual glare remains on the last free channel. At the transit the glared leg's M (the far origin's caller) is taken as a claim (R_LEG, net_unit.v:683-686). With one leg (rs_two) the incoming port already listens to the leg (the way back, net_unit.v:732-736), so the upstream origin also sees M rise on its trunk and 'claims' on the stranger's hook (net_unit.v:795-800). From then on it never times out. The resolver frees itself (net_unit.v:701-706). The upstream path is now held up by the stranger's hook through the transit's way back. (i) If the stranger's side drops (hangs up, own code, reserved digit, or its guard), the transit's in-port and the upstream trunk release themselves T_REL later on the fall of their fE/fM. (ii) Otherwise, when the transit's own monitor later claims the upstream call, the CLAIM write re-points the in-port from the glared leg (E up) to 00 (net_unit.v:656-658). Its fE falls, and T_REL later the port releases itself and clears CLM (port.v:183-186, 193). That generalises: any unit write that re-points a port whose E is up becomes a release T_REL later. The release runs back to the upstream trunk. In both cases both origins are 'claimed' and at the last digit connect their callers to trunks that have already released (net_unit.v:818-821).
findings.trigger: tb_pchain.v sc0 (scale 8): chain A 2 2 - B 2 3 - C 2 4, where the B-C link has one channel. A20 dials 1 2 3 2 1 (B21). C20 keys 1 timed so that C's origin and B's forward take B14-C11 unseen. Calibrated from two single keys (B14 written 41.3 ms after A's key, C11 27.3 ms after C's); glare on the first try with C's key 14.0 ms after A's (B14 and C11 both written at 2128.284 ms). Pass 0: the callers dial on 40 ms after C's key. Pass 1: 80 ms after.
findings.consequence: Pass 0: C20's first break fell inside C's 16 ms guard, so C abandoned. C11, B14, B11 and A11 then released one after another while A20 was still dialling. B's monitor cleared, and A's 'claimed' origin connected A20 to the released A11. Pass 1: B's monitor claimed A20's call correctly at b, and the CLAIM write re-pointed B11 off B14 (E up, C20's hook). B11 released 33 ms later, taking CLM, then A11, B14 and C11 followed. A20, who dialled B21 correctly, never reaches it. C20's call went nowhere. Both finish latched onto idle trunks (A20 -> A11, C20 -> C11, both released): silence, and whatever next seizes those channels is heard (the origin slice's S4 listen-in, work/audit/origin/run_s2_5.log). The hypothesised listen-in of C20 on A20's call did NOT happen, because the orphan leg released with the rest. At a hub the resolver would also drop the real legs on the glare leg's M, losing the call in every other branch. At real timers the stranger's M reaches the upstream origin about 15 ms after its seizure, inside the 128 ms guard, so the upstream origin counts EV_GLARE naming its own trunk, a link that never glared (at scale 8 it arrived just outside the 16 ms guard, so this run shows glare 0 at A).
findings.realistic: Residual glare only (see residual-glare-rate): the last free channel must be taken from both ends within about 1.3 ms. The mechanism uses no scaled timer except the guard that triggered pass 0. At real timers the release delays are 256 ms instead of 32, the stranger's departure is a hang-up, own code or reserved digit, and pass 1's self-release happens regardless.
findings.fix: (a) The origin re-checks its claim: after the claim it watches the claimed trunk's M, and if M falls before N_DONE it abandons with NOGO. It already compares the probe's port with d_trunk (net_unit.v:795-797), so this is one more term, and it also closes the origin slice's S4. (b) A resolver treats M on a leg within about 100 ms of writing it as glare, not a claim. A real claim needs two digits, so it cannot come that soon. It then writes that leg away instead of freeing itself; with (a) in place the far origin abandons cleanly. Cost: a small per-resolver age counter, about half a package each. (c) w_claim should also write the one-leg way back away. The general rule: never re-point a port whose E is up unless a release is intended.

findings.title: The 128 ms guard covers about 9 hops uncontended and 4 when transits are busy, not 'ten'; the RTL's hop is 12-14 ms, not 7
findings.mechanism: Per transit hop (all unscaled wiring timing): the classifier samples the rise at the port's turn, 0-1 ms (net_unit.v:283). The word read waits for the port's next turn plus 8 frames, about 1.1 ms (550-552, word_rx.v). The forward's sweep waits for port 1's turn, 0-1 ms, then makes 64 reads on a stride of 9 frames, 9 ms (453-454, 750-777). The confirm pass is 1 ms (779-785). The leg is written after the queue's WAIT of 156 us plus 133 us a word (225-232). The leg's E is captured at the incoming port's turn, 0-1 ms (port.v:173). The fwd slice measured this at real timers: 12.1-12.9 ms to the first leg's far M, 13.4-13.9 ms to the last of three (work/audit/fwd/run_fx_sc5.log). The origin's usable guard is t_guard - HIT from the push: the guard abandons on r_brk (net_unit.v:862), which comes HIT (8 ms) into a break (pulse_rx.v:84), and tmr starts at the seizure push (815). So a first break starting 120 ms after the push passes. Hop 1 (the push, the write and the caller's E capture) is 0.3-1.8 ms. A leg written during the caller's break presents its rise only at the break's end, and the far monitor then loses the first pulse. Load adds to a hop: a T_ARM watch on a previous seizure (net_unit.v:584-588 holds the classifier for T_ARM + 2 = 18 ms; measured 30.4 ms), the origin's sweep ahead of the forward (715; measured 18.4-25.5 ms), and about 1 ms per classifier or marker read that pre-empts a sweep read (292, 453).
findings.trigger: A caller whose pause after the key is just above the abandon threshold (ID 128 + origin sweep ~11 + guard 128, about 267 ms), calling across K hops. Floods from two origins within about 20 ms meet at every shared transit, and the second waits out the first's T_ARM watch.
findings.consequence: 128 ms tap: 10 hops at the best uncontended hop (12.1 ms), 9 at the worst (13.9), 6 with every transit behind an origin sweep, 4 with every transit behind a T_ARM watch. 256 ms tap: 18-21 / 11 / 9. network.md 3.2's planning rule of 'no more than about eight hops' holds only while at most one transit on the path is busy: 8 hops take 99 ms with none busy, 116 ms with one, 132 ms with two (over the 120 ms). Beyond the reach, the far monitor counts e short, and a code one pulse lower is claimed: a wrong number. The doc's '7 ms a hop' and 'a hub counts as a hop and a third' do not match either: a hub's extra legs cost about 1 ms, a twelfth of a hop.
findings.realistic: Real timing (the hop is wiring timing, measured at real timers by the fwd slice). It matters only for fast diallers (pause 267 ms up to roughly 267 ms + the depth excess). A conforming 720 ms pause leaves 40+ hops of room. The scale-8 benches cannot see any of this: their 16 ms guard covers less than one hop (tb_net.v header).
findings.evidence: Arithmetic on the fwd slice's measured hop latencies (run_fx_sc5.log: 'HOP 5a nominal: ... first 12.127-12.877 ms, last 13.150-13.900 ms', 'HOP 5b behind a T_ARM watch: ... 30.384 ms', 'HOP 5c behind an origin sweep: ... 18.383 / 22.383 ms', 'HOP 5d ... 24.524 ms'), and the RTL lines above. Table: K = 1 + floor((120 - first)/hop).
findings.fix: Plan on about 14 ms a hop plus about 17 ms per busy transit, and make the 256 ms tap the default for anything deeper than 4-5 hops. Cheapest RTL relief: take the T_ARM watch out of the classifier's critical path (a 2-entry watch list, so a second seizure is read at once rather than 18 ms later), and start the forward's sweep at the port after the incoming one rather than at port 1. Update monitor.md 3.5's table and network.md 3.2's timing row.

findings.title: Every forward, even a chain transit's one leg, holds a resolver for the whole flood, and with none free the seizure is not forwarded at all
findings.mechanism: A forward starts only if a resolver is free (net_unit.v:616-621, nf_busy 506-507). Every forward, one leg included (rs_two), takes a resolver (737-741). The resolver is held until the claim comes back through its leg (R_LEG) or the incoming port's BUSY falls (R_GONE), i.e. until the origin drops the trunk plus T_REL (681-708). The docs promise otherwise: network.md:176 'One found: patch it, two latches, and forget', :241-243 and :267-268 'a transit on a chain ... holds nothing', and :286 'no resolver free: patch into the first direction found'. The RTL has no such fallback.
findings.trigger: Any transit, chain or hub, while NRES = 2 floods are already in progress through it.
findings.consequence: The third concurrent flood through a transit is held but not passed on (n_nofwd). Every exchange beyond misses the call, and if the owner is beyond, the caller gets cannot-complete only at T_CLAIM (about 2 s after b, 4-5 s after the key). At real timers the resolver hold is about 2.5-5.5 s: to the claim, or to the drop plus 0.26 s, or to T_CLAIM for a failed call. A central transit sees every network flood. For the doc's 8-exchange network (348 lines, 30 % leaving, 0.087 floods/s): A = 0.26 E, 2.6 % of floods not forwarded per central transit (0.2 % with 3 resolvers). For 20 exchanges of 48 lines: 0.72 E, 13 % (3.0 % with 3, 0.55 % with 4). At 50 % leaving: 25 %. A call crossing k such transits is lost with 1-(1-B)^k. Graceful in kind (a clean cannot-complete, nothing stuck, never a wrong number) but slow.
findings.realistic: Real timers. The hold times are protocol digit times, not scaled wiring.
findings.evidence: RTL lines above. Erlang B on hold times read from the RTL. The fwd slice reproduced the pool running out ('sc4: resolver pool exhausted: floods held and not passed on', work/audit/fwd/run_fx_sc4.log).
findings.fix: The one-leg forward does need its leg remembered: for a local claim's drop (659-665) and as the safety net for a leg written on a seizure that dies inside T_ARM, whose leg then has no fE edge. So either (a) the docs change to 'a resolver at every transit, sized on all network floods: 3 at 8 exchanges, 4 at 20', or (b) keep a one-leg forward's leg in the monitor cell holding the incoming port (a '174 a cell) with a T_ARM watch on the leg, and reserve resolvers for fan-outs. Implement the doc's fallback only together with (b).

findings.title: Under overload a call that will fail holds its flood about 2 s longer than one that succeeds: positive feedback on links and resolvers
findings.mechanism: A successful call's losing legs are dropped at the claim (net_unit.v:800, 831-837), about 2.2-3.2 s after the key at real dialling, then T_REL. A call whose flood could not reach its owner is dropped only at T_CLAIM, 2 s after b (net_unit.v:882), i.e. 4.4-5.4 s after the key. That includes the trunk no forward could take, the resolver no transit had and the monitor no owner had. Nothing can end it sooner. A transit that cannot forward only counts it (nf_empty/nf_busy, 506-508). The doc's 'transit may claim to refuse' (network.md:203-206) is not built, and would be unsafe: a transit cannot know whether the owner is reachable through another direction of the origin, and its refusal claim would win the race against the real owner's. T_CLAIM's 2 s is sized for a 0.9 s carrier round trip (network.md:75). In this RTL the claim returns in milliseconds: the owner decides b at the same instant as the origin, the CLAIM write is about 0.3 ms, and the way back is about 1-2 ms a hop.
findings.trigger: A network near its link or resolver capacity: floods that fail hold every link they reached for T_CLAIM more.
findings.consequence: Flood occupancy grows by about 0.75 x the blocking fraction. Example: 20 exchanges of 48 lines, 30 % leaving, 2 central transits with NRES = 2. Blocking alone is 24 %; with the feedback the fixed point is about 32 %. Retries amplify it. It is not a livelock or a collapse (every hold is bounded), but it is ungraceful: resources are held longest by calls that will fail. The caller hears cannot-complete about 2 s after b.
findings.realistic: Real timers. The magnitude depends on the carrier mix: with copper and MF8 only, T_CLAIM could be much shorter.
findings.evidence: RTL lines above; arithmetic (fixed point of A = lambda (3 s (1-p) + 5 s p), p = 1-(1-B(2,A))^2).
findings.fix: Make T_CLAIM a jumpered tap like the guard: about 500 ms for copper and MF8 networks (covers the owner's b + ID + CLAIM write + a S_WATCH SETTLE wait + the path), 2 s only where a slow carrier needs it. No parts, one tap. Do not build the transit refusal.

findings.title: With the mini marker's one register, the owner refuses roughly 1 incoming network call in 6, and two exchanges calling each other both fail
findings.mechanism: A claim is taken only if the owner's register is free (mini_marker.v:273-274). Otherwise it is refused to 03 with CLM (320-327). The register is held by any caller from lift to connect, and by an outgoing network caller until N_DONE, i.e. through all five digits (net_unit.v:881, mini_marker S_YIELD). The refusal is heard only after the origin's N_DONE, because the caller sits on SILENCE until then (net_unit.v:818-821), so monitor.md:64's 'hears it at once' does not hold.
findings.trigger: Any incoming network call while the owner's register is busy. Deterministically, A calls B while B calls A with keys within about two digit-times.
findings.consequence: Register occupancy at a 48-line exchange (3 calls a line an hour; local ~3 s, outgoing network ~7 s, incoming claim ~2 s) is about 0.19-0.23 E, so 16-19 % of incoming network calls get cannot-complete. Crossing calls between two exchanges: both refused (the origin slice reproduced it: work/audit/origin/run_s2_5.log 'OBS S2: ... refusals A 1 B 1'). Graceful (clean cannot-complete, nothing held), but it dominates every other loss in this build.
findings.realistic: Real dialling times. This is the known 'one register' limit, quantified.
findings.evidence: RTL lines above; Erlang with one server, B = A/(1+A); origin slice S2.
findings.fix: A register pool (the class-marker build), or at least a second register on the mini marker reserved for claims. Correct monitor.md 2's 'at once'.

findings.title: Residual glare: window about 1.35 ms per end, and rate against load for 2- and 8-channel groups
findings.mechanism: Glare needs both ends to take the same channel after each end's confirm visit (net_unit.v:779-785) and before the other end's M arrives. The per-end window D runs from the confirm visit to the far port's M: the rest of the 1 ms confirm pass (mean 0.5 ms), plus WAIT 156 us and a 133 us word, plus the E capture (mean 0.5 ms), plus the card's 31 us. That is about 1.35 ms mean and 2.7 ms worst. g makes the two ends start from opposite ends of the group, so it needs the last free channel. Forwards count as seizures at each end too, so a central link sees every network flood from both sides.
findings.trigger: Opposite-end seizures within about +/-1.35 ms while exactly one channel is free.
findings.consequence: Estimated glare rate = 2 x P(one free) x lambda_X x lambda_Y x 2D (holding about 8 s mixed floods/calls). 2-channel link: 0.2 E -> 1 per 2000 h; 0.5 E -> 1 per 170 h; 1.0 E (20 % blocked) -> 1 per 33 h. 8-channel link: 2 E -> 1 per 960 h; 4 E -> 1 per 14 h; 6 E -> 1 per 2 h; 8 E offered -> about 1 an hour. Negligible at design loads, but daily-to-hourly under overload on a busy central link. Each event is two joined callers, or forward-glare-collapse. On the counters it shows as EV_GLARE on an origin's trunk even when the glare was hops away.
findings.realistic: Real timing. The window is wiring timing, identical at both scales. tb_lfull and tb_pchain both glared on their first try with synchronised keys.
findings.evidence: Arithmetic on the RTL's confirm-to-write path. tb_pchain glare at try 0 (run_pchain.log); tb_lfull glare at try 0 (work/base-lfull.log 'glare at try 0, B's key 0 us after A's').
findings.fix: None needed at design load. If it matters under overload, keep one channel per group as glare reserve (seize the last free channel only from the g end), about one gate on the sweep's g compare.

findings.title: Jumpering only one end of a ring link does not stop double delivery: the unjumpered end forwards the other end's own floods round the ring
findings.mechanism: The ring strap is per direction at each unit. A seizure is not forwarded onward if it arrived on a strapped direction (net_unit.v:616), and never forwarded into one (fwd_mask, 505, 618). An origin seizes every direction, strapped or not (h_mask 1111, 849). With the strap only at X's end of link L = X-Y, X's own origin seizures into L arrive at Y on an UNSTRAPPED port and Y forwards them onward round the ring. Every ring member then receives X's calls from both sides. network.md:352-355 says 'One end alone breaks the cycle just as well ... but ... wastes a channel', which is true of the cycle but not of double delivery.
findings.trigger: A ring with the jumper fitted at one end of the chosen link only; any call originated at the jumpered end.
findings.consequence: Every call from X reaches every ring member twice, which is network.md 3.3's own 'race no caller should be in': two monitors per call, and a double claim at the owner. One copy takes the register and the other is refused to 03 with CLM. The origin keeps whichever claim M rises first, and the refused copy can win by a millisecond, giving cannot-complete (see sound: double claim). It also uses twice the monitors and channels. Never a wrong number.
findings.realistic: Planning or configuration error; the doc currently permits it.
findings.evidence: RTL reading, lines above. The double-claim mechanics at the jumpered link's ends were reproduced by the origin slice (work/audit/origin/run_s2_5.log S5: 'B refusals 1').
findings.fix: Doc: 'both ends MUST be jumpered'. Optionally a strap mismatch check: an EV word when a seizure arrives on a direction whose word says the far end is strapped. That needs a bit in the trunk word; not worth it.

findings.title: The whole idle/hold convention assumes port 00 is never fitted; nothing enforces it
findings.mechanism: Holds, drops, releases and 'silence' all point a port at 00 (net_unit.v:592, 610, 662, 697, 826, 834; port.v:193; mini_marker SILENCE = 00). The resulting E, and the backward A before a claim, is 0 only because 00 is empty: /HA at bit-time 0 idles high (port.v:88, 173). site_net.v:97-99 fits block 0 if LTU[0] is set, and PHONES bit 0 would fit 00. exch.v/block.v accept any PORT_FITTED. The classifier skips 00 (net_unit.v:284), which suggests it is known.
findings.trigger: A card fitted at 00, e.g. a local trunk unit on block 0 (forbidden for MF8 by mf8-unit.md:58, not for the local trunk).
findings.consequence: Every hold would send 00's M as backward A, so every origin takes it as a claim: wrong numbers everywhere. Every idle phone (listening to 00) would ring whenever 00's M is up.
findings.realistic: Assembly or configuration error only.
findings.evidence: RTL reading.
findings.fix: Mask PORT_FITTED[0] to 0 in exch.v, or put a lint check in site_net/top. On the board, do not stuff position 0 of block 0 (no socket).

findings.title: A leaf (one direction) runs a full 10 ms forward sweep for every incoming flood and counts it as 'not forwarded'
findings.mechanism: fwd_mask excludes only the incoming direction and the strapped ones (net_unit.v:505, 618). The unit has no record of which directions exist, so at a leaf fwd_mask is non-zero, F_WANT starts a sweep (714-719), it finds nothing (h_ok = 0, 722), and nf_empty increments n_nofwd (508, 545).
findings.trigger: Every incoming flood at an end-of-chain or leaf exchange.
findings.consequence: The leaf's own origin can wait up to 10 ms more for the sweep (net_unit.v:848), and a sweep in progress delays classifier and marker reads by about 1 ms each. n_nofwd counts normal events, so it cannot serve as a loss counter or alarm.
findings.realistic: Every incoming call at every leaf; cheap but constant.
findings.evidence: RTL reading.
findings.fix: A 4-bit 'directions present' register, set by every sweep for every trunk word read, free or not (at 759), and cleared by a sweep that reads none. Skip the forward when fwd_mask & present == 0. One '175 and gates.

findings.title: Drop-then-reseize is closed only by 0.1-0.3 ms on baseband and local trunks; a carrier with a slower-falling A reopens it
findings.mechanism: When one end drops a trunk, it stays BUSY for T_REL through its fE (port.v:147). The far port releases on its fM fall T_REL after the same edge. The two ends free within +/-1 tick plus the A path's fall delay: independent 1 ms ticks give up to 1.03 ms apart. A re-seizure from the end that freed first reaches the far port no sooner than about 1.32 ms later: the read, a full 1 ms confirm pass, WAIT plus a word, the card. With /UREQ already held the WAIT is skipped. Margin 0.13-0.29 ms. If the carrier's A falls about 1-2 ms slower than it rises, as with network.md's MF8 figures of 1.5 ms up and 2 ms down, the new seizure's M rises while the far port is still BUSY. Its fM never falls, the old hold stays (st set, never classified), and the new flood dies there. If the old monitor cell had not yet reached CLR, it counts on (the monclaim slice's stale cell).
findings.trigger: A link whose A falls slower than it rises; a channel dropped at one end and re-seized from the same end in the next sweep.
findings.consequence: Lost calls; at worst the stale-cell miscount.
findings.realistic: Not reachable with the RTL's baseband or local-trunk cards. It is a latent constraint on any future carrier (MF8, the pots trunk).
findings.evidence: Reasoning from port.v and net_unit.v:750-785 timing.
findings.fix: Record in network.md 1.1: a carrier's A fall and rise delays must match within about 0.1 ms, or the sweep must skip a port for about 2 ms after it frees.

findings.title: Smaller places where the documents and the RTL disagree
findings.mechanism: (1) monitor.md:197 says the marker reads M rising inside the guard 'as glare and not as a claim'. net_unit.v:795-804 takes it as the claim and counts glare, as network.md 1 ('residual glare joins two callers') and tb_lfull expect. (2) monitor.md 3 rule 1 says a monitor gets a seizure 'within one scan of its rise ... or not at all'. The RTL attaches it whenever the classifier gets to it (net_unit.v:262-273, 283-284): 1-3 ms normally, 18-20 ms behind a T_ARM watch, more in a burst, and relies on the guard instead (counted in guard-reach). (3) network.md:53 says a released trunk is held busy for about 0.6 s. The RTL's settle is each port's own T_REL (256 ms, port.v:147). (4) network.md 3.1/4's 7 ms hop and 3.2's 'hub counts as a hop and a third' do not match: 12-14 ms, and about +1 ms. (5) network.md 3.3 'the direct copy always claims first': both copies carry the same live pulses and complete within a millisecond or so of each other; the tie is broken by monitor cell order (net_unit.v:335-337).
findings.trigger: n/a
findings.consequence: Planning figures in the docs are optimistic, and one statement (1) is internally contradictory.
findings.realistic: n/a
findings.evidence: Lines cited.
findings.fix: Edit the docs to the RTL's figures.

findings.title: The scale-8 network benches cannot test the guard's reach, and they overstate the single forwarder's losses
findings.mechanism: At scale 8 the guard is 16 ms against a 12-14 ms unscaled hop, so it covers about one hop (tb_net.v:49-55 says so). The classifier's T_ARM watch is 4 ms instead of 18, so a second seizure within about 5 ms reaches w_cls while the forwarder is still sweeping and is not forwarded. At real timers the 18 ms watch serialises it until the forwarder is free, unless an origin sweep delayed the forwarder (the fwd slice's 5d). Link-outage and glare timings also shift.
findings.trigger: n/a
findings.consequence: The green scale-8 benches say nothing about multi-hop wrong-number safety. Crossing-flood losses seen at scale 8 are mostly absent at real timers. Conversely, the real-timer 18 ms serialisation (guard-reach) is invisible at scale 8.
findings.realistic: n/a
findings.evidence: Parameters in tb_net.v/tb_chain.v; work/audit/fwd/run_fx_sc5.log 5b/5d.
findings.fix: Keep at least one real-timer multi-hop bench, with a 3-4 hop chain and a first break at 129 ms, in the sequence (tb_pflap here runs 2 exchanges at real timers in about 15 min).

sound.claim: g protects a forwarder exactly as it protects an origin.
sound.why: Both use the one sweep, with the same per-candidate g compare on the word read (net_unit.v:759-766) and the same confirm pass (779-785). Residual glare needs the last free channel whoever hunts.

sound.claim: Crossing floods (A->C with C->A through B, A->B with B->A) cannot take each other's claim.
sound.why: The origin watches only its own d_trunk ports (net_unit.v:795-797), resolvers only their own legs (683-686), and 'mine' keeps the classifier off every port the unit seized (429-438). The only cross-coupling is glare on a shared link (forward-glare-collapse). The calls do contend for the one forwarder and the one register (one-register-refuses-claims).

sound.claim: Backward A is 0 before any claim on every top_net build with port 00 unfitted.
sound.why: Holds listen to 00 with CLM 0 (net_unit.v:610); a one-leg way back carries the next hop's hold (also 0); drops and releases point at 00 (592, 662, 697, 826, 834; port.v:193). The only pre-claim sources are glare, a stuck-1 conductor (phantom-seizure-no-timeout) and a fitted 00 (port00-must-be-unfitted).

sound.claim: The claim is a level carried through every patch.
sound.why: A claimed port's a_rx = E || CLM (port.v:153). The one-leg way back is written with the forward (net_unit.v:732-736); a hub's way back is written at R_LEG (701-705); the marker keeps CLM on every write to a claimed trunk (mini_marker ctx_clm). tb_chain and tb_lchain end-to-end calls pass. The exception is a re-point of a port whose E is up (forward-glare-collapse).

sound.claim: Release propagates hop by hop without false seizures, including when the called party hangs up first at a transit.
sound.why: Each port clears on its own fall, and a released port with standing M is protected by st (net_unit.v:262-277, 566-570; set by M under BUSY). Release proceeds in T_REL steps back along the chain; tb_net scenario 2 covers one hop and the same argument applies per hop.

sound.claim: A dropped trunk cannot be re-seized while the far end still holds it (baseband and local trunk).
sound.why: The dropping end stays BUSY through its fE for T_REL (port.v:147), and the far end releases on the same edge within about 1 tick; a re-seizure needs about 1.32 ms or more (confirm pass plus write). Margin 0.13-0.29 ms; see release-margin-thin for carriers where it fails.

sound.claim: A claim cannot race a forward still in progress at the same transit.
sound.why: A claim needs two digits after the seizure (1.5 s or more at real dialling, 240 ms or more at scale 8); the forward takes 12-30 ms and starts only at w_cls (net_unit.v:616-621).

sound.claim: A claim racing the caller's hang-up, or arriving after T_CLAIM, is released cleanly.
sound.why: The origin drops every held trunk (net_unit.v:823-829); the owner's register sees CLR on the trunk and writes it free (mini_marker S_COLLECT r_gone); a refused trunk releases on its fM fall. Nothing is left BUSY, apart from the 1-tick window noted in the monclaim/cableb slices.

sound.claim: Double claim at the ends of a jumpered link: the losing copy is released.
sound.why: The first claim takes the register and the second is refused to 03 with CLM (mini_marker.v:320-327); the origin keeps the first M rise and drops the other at once (net_unit.v:800, 831-837); the refused port releases on its fM fall (origin slice S5). Caveat: which copy wins at the owner is the monitor cell order on a same-tick tie, and the refused copy's backward A can reach the origin first, giving cannot-complete, never a wrong number (doc-drift item 5).

sound.claim: Plesiochronous links cannot make or lose a pulse.
sound.why: A crosses a baseband card through two flip-flops on the local frame edge (baseband_card.v:139-140), and a local trunk through a cell register and a frame-edge crossing (local_trunk.v:164-176); a slip is a one-frame (15.6 us) level glitch. The ports and counters sample once per ms and HIT is 8 samples. Word reads are local to the card. tb_lnet/tb_lchain run at 100 ppm.

sound.claim: The claim's round trip fits inside T_CLAIM with a large margin.
sound.why: The owner decides b at the same tick-quantised instant as the origin; CLAIM is written at once, before att (net_unit.v:656-673); the way back is about 1-2 ms a hop. Only a second claim waiting behind the att handshake can be late (S_WATCH, cableb slice).

sound.claim: A long outage releases cleanly, and the dead trunk leaves the hunt.
sound.why: The card forces A to 0 and floats the word (baseband_card.v:154,157; local_trunk.v:188-192); the ports release after T_REL; the sweep keeps only trunk words (net_unit.v:759). A hunt that read the word just before the fall seizes a dead trunk: no claim, cannot-complete at T_CLAIM. The exception is a link that returns while the caller still dials (link-return-fresh-seizure).

sound.claim: The T_ARM hold watch covers the whole arming window of the incoming port.
sound.why: The hold is written 1.4 ms or more after the rise; C_HOLD watches until T_ARM + 2 ticks after the write (net_unit.v:584-588); the port's fM rises exactly T_ARM after the rise (port.v:178-181). A fall inside the window is always sampled (once a ms). The hole it opens for dial breaks is the cableb slice's tb_brk.

sound.claim: The one-leg transit's leg cannot be left with no edge.
sound.why: If the incoming seizure dies before the leg's fE arms, R_GONE fires when the incoming port's BUSY falls (by its own fM, or by C_UNHOLD) and writes the leg away (net_unit.v:688-698). This is also why a chain forward needs a resolver (chain-forward-holds-resolver).
